summary:
Syria is a country trans visitors should not enter. The fall of the Assad regime in December 2024 did not disturb the statutory framework that governs a visitor's exposure: Penal Code Article 520 prohibits "carnal relations against the order of nature" with up to three years' imprisonment, and Article 517 criminalises public indecency. Outright International's country overview, updated 12 March 2026, records that both provisions are applied to women as well as men, so a trans visitor is reachable by the same articles irrespective of legal sex marker or presentation.

The same overview records that legal gender recognition is impossible in Syria and that LGBTI organisations cannot register. There is no anti-discrimination protection of any kind; the state's answer to same-sex conduct is criminalisation, which removes the complaint route a visitor would otherwise have after an incident.

The security position has worsened since December 2024. The Guardians of Equality Movement (GEM) worked through an on-the-ground reporter network and documented waves of violence against Syrian transgender women across the first two months of 2025, with non-state armed groups and security forces implicated in several cities. GEM also circulated video footage from February 2025 showing authorities detaining trans women. Any state actor or armed group operating today can act against a trans visitor under the provisions that remain in force.

Violence by armed groups is documented alongside state action. A Human Rights Watch report of 16 April 2018 (updated 30 August 2021) tallied at least 16 killings in Syria claimed by ISIS for alleged sodomy as of June 2016, against 23 in Iraq and 3 in Libya. A separate record in the same inventory states that ISIS reported executing at least 30 people for "sodomy" in the areas it controlled, and that Hay'at Tahrir al-Sham and the Islamic State carried out beatings and torture of LGBTQ people. The killings were reported to the UN Security Council in August 2015, in the Council's first-ever discussion of LGBTQ concerns.

State enforcement has precedent inside Syria itself. In June 2010 Syrian authorities raided a series of private parties over preceding weeks and arrested more than 25 men, most charged with "homosexual acts" and others with drug offences; the charges later listed also included encouraging homosexual behaviour and organising obscene parties. Private gatherings are therefore not a safe setting.

Political actors across the spectrum have publicly endorsed harsher treatment. A Free Syrian Army member stated he would enforce tougher laws and would not object to stoning homosexuals, and a secular leader said Syrian society would answer "no way" to gays claiming rights. Such statements from armed and political figures are not historical curiosities in a country where armed formations still hold coercive power.
tangentialFactors:
Reporting discipline is uneven, and the visitor should treat single-source claims with care. GEM's April 2025 report investigated a claim circulating at the time that LGBTQIA individuals were being hunted and targeted in Homs, and found it inaccurate through its reporter network, stating the claim risked stirring incitement against the community. That finding does not negate the documented pattern of attacks on trans women in early 2025; it does mean that viral allegations should not be taken as established fact in either direction.

The European Union Agency for Asylum's Syria country-focus entry on treatment by state, non-state and societal actors yielded no usable finding for this record, so the assessment rests on the sources named here rather than on an asylum-authority risk determination.

Public cultural expression has been squeezed since the civil war. The region's only gay tour, which ran in Damascus and Aleppo, stopped operating, and the underground LGBTQ hubs of the capital were eradicated; the tour's organiser had described the hammams of Aleppo and Damascus as venues where "we never had any problems." Digital expression continues anonymously: the "One of you" movement began on Facebook in March 2020 and moved to Twitter, with university students painting LGBTQ flag colours on their fingers and photographing themselves under #oneofyou, most using fake accounts for fear of identification. Reactions ranged from defence to threats of blood before the movement faded amid COVID-19.

Refugee testimony has been carried to international bodies. In 2015 two gay refugees from Syria and Iraq testified at the first-ever meeting on LGBT rights at the UN Security Council, a closed session co-sponsored by the United States and Chile, describing constant fear of violence and death under authoritarian governments, militant groups and ISIS; activists also brought the ISIS killings to the Council's attention.

In the diaspora, Syrian LGBTQ+ refugees face discrimination and exclusion in host countries on grounds of race, language, skin colour and religious background. The 2017 film Mr. Gay Syria follows two gay Syrian refugees rebuilding their lives, and Abdulrahman Akkad, a Syrian young man in Germany who came out publicly on Facebook in July 2017 under family pressure to marry against his will, had his case raised in the German Parliament's 2020 human rights session.
localsOnly:
Residents have no registration route for advocacy. LGBTI organisations cannot register with the state, and no anti-discrimination protection exists, so complaints about employment, housing or services have no statutory basis.

Legal gender recognition is impossible. Syrians have no procedure to amend the sex marker on civil documents, which affects interaction with every state service that reads those records.

Health care is shaped by official stigma as well as under-provision. In 2005 the Deputy Minister of Religious Endowments publicly called HIV/AIDS "divine punishment" for fornication and homosexuality, while the Health Ministry claimed only 369 people were infected and offered free medicines, a figure NGOs estimated at least five times too low, and the UN chastised the government for ineffective prevention. The state runs voluntary HIV testing clinics, distributes pamphlets, tolerates the work of some NGOs, and offers a limited HIV/AIDS educational programme for youth in secondary schooling, but comprehensive public education for LGBTQ people does not exist.

Reported prevalence is low: under 2 per 100,000 in the general population and under 1% among most-at-risk populations in 2018, with 1,013 cases reported through Q3 2019 since the first reported infections in 1987. Physical safety is itself a barrier to care, with beatings and torture of LGBTQ people recorded frequently.

Expression remains chilled at home. In Damascus homosexuality and "public decency" offences are illegal, and a 36-year-old resident, Amira al-Tabbaa, described living "only in whispers" when meeting friends in gay-friendly cafes. Young people who campaigned publicly did so through fake accounts.
outOfScopeNotes:
The casualty tallies for ISIS killings of men accused of sodomy in Syria are not reconciled in the sources: Human Rights Watch records at least 16 claimed killings as of June 2016, while another record states ISIS reported executing at least 30 people for "sodomy" in its areas. The discrepancy is unresolved here and may reflect different counting periods or inclusion of pre-2016 events.

Whether the fall of the Assad regime in December 2024 changed the text or penalties of Penal Code Articles 520 and 517 is not sourced in this inventory. The assessment treats the articles as operative on the strength of Outright International's overview updated 12 March 2026, but a current consolidated Penal Code has not been consulted.

No source in this inventory addresses entry and visa rules for trans visitors, airport or border screening that could expose a traveller's documents, the treatment of foreign versus Syrian citizenship at the border, or the availability of consular assistance. Those points are not sourced rather than confirmed as safe.

The inventory carries no trans-specific judicial decision, sentence or acquittal after December 2024, and no named case of a foreign national prosecuted under Article 520. Enforcement figures for the current period are likewise absent; the pre-2011 and civil-war-era incidents are the only quantified enforcement records available.

Sub-national variation is barely covered. GEM's early 2025 findings reference several cities, and a debunked claim centred on Homs is noted, but no source establishes which authorities currently control enforcement in which governorate.
